network.overall_strategy: Threonine is treated as a late, low-flux surface product accessed through the only two reaction families with meaningful experimental support: a cyanosulfidic Strecker branch that builds the bottleneck precursor lactaldehyde and traps it as a threonine aminonitrile, and a Cu-assisted Akabori aldol branch that couples acetaldehyde with pre-existing glycine in concentrated, cooler surface pools. The network keeps allothreonine explicit as the unavoidable coproduct, treats acetaldehyde and lactaldehyde as bottlenecks, and includes retro-aldol cleavage back to glycine plus acetaldehyde because threonine is fragile and poorly suited to hydrothermal accumulation. The 10 pathways are entry variants into these two modules rather than 10 independent origin frameworks.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin capture of formaldehyde to glycolonitrile

conditions.other: cyanide-bearing evaporitic or tidal-flat pool; wet-dry concentration; anoxic

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to formaldehyde to give the cyanohydrin glycolonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This entry step is a simplifying but chemically standard abstraction. The cited cyanosulfidic literature reaches the same glycolonitrile node by longer HCN homologation chemistry, whereas direct formaldehyde cyanohydrin capture is used here to expose the threonine-relevant network without adding unrelated upstream steps (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Cu-sulfide photoreduction of glycolonitrile to glycolaldehyde

conditions.other: UV-irradiated sulfidic pool, phosphate-buffered near pH 7; elemental sulfur is a bookkeeping sink for oxidized sulfur

reactions.mechanism: UV-driven Cu-mediated sulfide photoredox reduces the nitrile carbon to an aldehyde equivalent and hydrolyzes the reduced intermediate, releasing ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson and Sutherland showed CuCN/phosphate/HS- plus UV can reduce nitrile-derived intermediates toward aldehydes. This net step captures glycolonitrile-to-glycolaldehyde conversion; sulfur is shown as elemental S only as a bookkeeping sink because the true oxidized sulfur pool is more complex. Sulfide supply and UV attenuation remain important geochemical constraints (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015; Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Cu-sulfide photoreduction of glycolaldehyde to acetaldehyde

conditions.other: same UV/sulfidic surface setting as rxn_002; phosphate-buffered; anoxic

reactions.mechanism: Related Cu-sulfide photoredox reduces and deoxygenates glycolaldehyde to acetaldehyde, with sulfide serving as reductant and sulfur as the bookkeeping oxidation sink.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. place acetaldehyde downstream of glycolaldehyde reduction in the same cyanosulfidic framework. This is a decisive hub-forming step because acetaldehyde feeds both the Strecker and Akabori branches; sulfur speciation is again simplified to S for a balanceable net reaction (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation from acetaldehyde to lactonitrile

conditions.other: HCN-rich, mildly alkaline to neutral surface pool

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to acetaldehyde to form the cyanohydrin lactonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Acetaldehyde cyanohydrin formation is straightforward aqueous cyanide chemistry and gives lactonitrile, the immediate photoredox precursor to lactaldehyde. Cobb and Pudritz identify lactaldehyde as threonine's Strecker aldehyde, so this step is central rather than optional (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Cobb & Pudritz, 2015).

reactions.name: Cu-sulfide photoreduction of lactonitrile to lactaldehyde

conditions.other: UV-irradiated sulfidic pool, phosphate-buffered near pH 7; reported lactaldehyde yield about 19 percent

reactions.mechanism: Photoredox reduction converts the nitrile carbon of lactonitrile to the aldehyde level with hydrolytic ammonia release; sulfide is oxidized to a sulfur pool represented here as elemental sulfur.
reactions.reasoning: This is the best documented threonine-specific bottleneck. Ritson and Sutherland reported lactonitrile photoreduction to lactaldehyde in about 19 percent yield under CuCN/HS-/UV conditions, making it the strongest experimental entry to threonine's required C3 hydroxyaldehyde precursor. The narrow geochemical window for sulfide and copper remains a real limitation (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015; Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Strecker capture of lactaldehyde to threonine aminonitrile

conditions.other: cool cyanide-ammonia-rich surface pool; imine formation followed by cyanide addition; mixed stereochemistry expected

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia condenses with lactaldehyde to an imine, then cyanide adds to give a stereochemically mixed threonine aminonitrile pool with water loss.
reactions.reasoning: Lactaldehyde plus HCN and NH3 is the canonical Strecker capture for threonine. The cited work reports smooth formation of the threonine aminonitrile pool from this aldehyde, but not a free-amino-acid yield or a resolved threo:allo aminonitrile ratio, so the product is modeled as a mixed aminonitrile node (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of threonine aminonitrile to threonine

conditions.other: dark rehydrating surface pool or evaporite film; implied stoichiometry is one aminonitrile plus two waters to one amino acid plus ammonia; low flux

reactions.mechanism: Stepwise nitrile hydration and hydrolysis converts the threonine aminonitrile branch to free threonine with ammonia release.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis to free threonine is chemically reasonable but experimentally the weakest part of the dedicated cyanosulfidic route: the provided literature stops at the aminonitrile stage and does not report a prebiotic free-threonine yield. This branch is therefore low-confidence and low-flux. It is kept because threonine is the target and because nonenzymatic threo:allo outcomes are unresolved rather than selectively threo (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015; Ring et al., 1972; Weber & Miller, 1981).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of threonine aminonitrile to allothreonine

conditions.other: dark rehydrating surface pool or evaporite film; implied stoichiometry is one aminonitrile plus two waters to one amino acid plus ammonia; low flux

reactions.mechanism: The parallel hydrolysis branch converts the aminonitrile pool to allothreonine with ammonia release.
reactions.reasoning: A separate allothreonine hydrolysis branch is required because nonenzymatic Strecker chemistry lacks useful diastereocontrol and abiotic threo:allo outcomes are often close to nonselective. As with rxn_007, the hydrolysis itself is chemically plausible but not experimentally secured for this specific aminonitrile under clearly prebiotic conditions (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015; Ring et al., 1972; Weber & Miller, 1981).

reactions.name: Cu-assisted glycine-acetaldehyde aldol to threonine

conditions.other: concentrated evaporitic pool or mineral interface; mildly basic carbonate or phosphate; low free sulfide so copper remains available; reversible Akabori-type chemistry

reactions.mechanism: Cu-chelated glycine undergoes C-alpha deprotonation and aldol addition to acetaldehyde to give threonine; the reaction is reversible.
reactions.reasoning: This Akabori-type aldol route is the only literature chemistry that intentionally reaches free threonine. Copper glycinate and related metal-chelate systems give threonine together with allothreonine, showing that the reaction is real even if the required Cu-rich, mildly basic, relatively low-sulfide pools may have been spatially restricted. It is included as a plausible low-water-activity surface route, but with lower prebiotic confidence than the precursor-supply photoredox chemistry (Sato et al., 1957; Ikutani et al., 1959).

reactions.name: Cu-assisted glycine-acetaldehyde aldol to allothreonine

conditions.other: concentrated evaporitic pool or mineral interface; mildly basic carbonate or phosphate; low free sulfide so copper remains available; reversible Akabori-type chemistry

reactions.mechanism: The same Cu-assisted glycine-acetaldehyde aldol chemistry can terminate in the allothreonine diastereomer.
reactions.reasoning: Allothreonine is an unavoidable parallel outcome in the same Cu-assisted glycine-acetaldehyde chemistry. Separate threo and allo branches are necessary because reported diastereomer ratios vary with catalyst and conditions rather than approaching exclusive threonine formation (Sato et al., 1957; Ikutani et al., 1959).

reactions.name: Retro-aldol cleavage of threonine to glycine and acetaldehyde

conditions.other: warm surface pool or geothermal cycling; decomposition sink accelerates with heating and long residence times

reactions.mechanism: Retro-aldol cleavage of the beta-hydroxy amino acid regenerates glycine and acetaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Retro-aldol cleavage of threonine back to glycine plus acetaldehyde is a major abiotic sink and explains why threonine should be treated as a late, low-accumulation product. Thermal studies and decomposition work show strong fragility with increasing temperature, arguing against prolonged hot residence (Schroeder & Bada, 1977; Aubrey et al., 2009).

reactions.name: Retro-aldol cleavage of allothreonine to glycine and acetaldehyde

conditions.other: warm surface pool or geothermal cycling; decomposition sink accelerates with heating and long residence times

reactions.mechanism: Allothreonine undergoes the same retro-aldol cleavage framework to regenerate glycine and acetaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Allothreonine should feed the same retro-aldol sink network as threonine, with additional blurring from epimerization. This branch is somewhat more inferential than rxn_011 but follows the documented threo-allo decomposition and epimerization behavior and is needed to keep the stereochemical pool chemically closed (Schroeder & Bada, 1977; Aubrey et al., 2009).

pathways.name: Full formaldehyde-to-threonine cyanosulfidic Strecker route
pathways.description: Formaldehyde is trapped as glycolonitrile, reduced through glycolaldehyde and acetaldehyde to lactonitrile and lactaldehyde, then captured as threonine aminonitrile and hydrolyzed in a cool dark surface pool.

pathways.name: Glycolonitrile-entry Strecker route
pathways.description: Begins at the experimentally central glycolonitrile node and follows the same acetaldehyde-lactaldehyde bottleneck to threonine aminonitrile and then threonine.

pathways.name: Glycolaldehyde-entry Strecker route
pathways.description: Starts from glycolaldehyde, bypasses the first cyanohydrin-capture step, and proceeds through acetaldehyde, lactonitrile, lactaldehyde, and the aminonitrile pool.

pathways.name: Acetaldehyde-entry Strecker route
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde supplied exogenously or by surface photochemistry enters the lactonitrile-lactaldehyde Strecker branch and then the hydrolysis step to threonine.

pathways.name: Lactonitrile-entry Strecker route
pathways.description: Late-entry route from lactonitrile, the immediate photoredox precursor of lactaldehyde and the most specific pre-threonine cyanohydrin node.

pathways.name: Lactaldehyde-entry Strecker route
pathways.description: Shortest chemically grounded Strecker route beginning from threonine's canonical aldehyde precursor, lactaldehyde.

pathways.name: Aminonitrile-completion route
pathways.description: A late completion pathway in which the accumulated threonine aminonitrile pool hydrolyzes to free threonine in a cool rehydrating surface setting.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde-derived acetaldehyde plus glycine Akabori route
pathways.description: Formaldehyde is converted to acetaldehyde by the cyanosulfidic surface module; acetaldehyde then condenses with pre-existing or recycled glycine in a less-sulfidic Cu-bearing evaporitic pool to give threonine directly.

pathways.name: Glycolaldehyde-derived acetaldehyde plus glycine Akabori route
pathways.description: A shorter aldol path in which glycolaldehyde first reduces to acetaldehyde, which then reacts with pre-existing or recycled glycine in the Cu-assisted aldol branch.

pathways.name: Direct glycine-acetaldehyde Akabori route
pathways.description: The shortest direct route to free threonine: glycine and acetaldehyde meet in a concentrated Cu-bearing surface pool and undergo reversible Akabori-type aldol chemistry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Literature-aware full cyanosulfidic route, but the end-to-end sequence compounds several low-yield steps and ends with the weakest step, rxn_007. The lactonitrile -> lactaldehyde -> aminonitrile segment is reasonably supported, but free threonine release is not demonstrated in the cited prebiotic work. rxn_007 should be corrected to mol_012 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_014 + mol_002; competing rxn_008 needs the same fix.
suggestions: Specify Cu species, UV regime, sulfide level, and phosphate/pH for rxn_002-rxn_005.
Rewrite rxn_007 as mol_012 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_014 + mol_002 and consider adding an amide hydrolysis intermediate.
Annotate expected threo:allo outcomes and cumulative yields.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Stronger than P1 because it bypasses formaldehyde capture, but it still depends on under-specified photoredox steps and the unvalidated hydrolysis in rxn_007. This route aligns with the cited cyanosulfidic logic, yet it still stops at the same experimental gap between aminonitrile and free threonine.
suggestions: Tie rxn_002-rxn_005 more explicitly to literature-supported Cu/H2S/UV/phosphate conditions.
Correct rxn_007 stoichiometry and specify the hydrolysis regime needed to reach free threonine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: By entering at glycolaldehyde this route avoids one upstream step, but confidence still rests on rxn_003/rxn_005 being run under the right Cu-assisted sulfidic photoredox conditions and on the weakly supported rxn_007 hydrolysis. The core acetaldehyde -> lactonitrile -> lactaldehyde -> aminonitrile sequence is coherent.
suggestions: Clarify whether rxn_003 is meant as direct photoreduction or shorthand for the documented cyanosulfidic photoredox manifold.
Correct and condition rxn_007, ideally with an explicit hydrolysis intermediate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Strongest Strecker entry variant. Acetaldehyde cyanohydrin formation is straightforward, rxn_005 has direct literature support for lactaldehyde formation, and rxn_006 matches the reported aminonitrile capture. The main weakness is rxn_007: hydrolysis to free threonine is not demonstrated in the cited cyanosulfidic work and needs 2 H2O stoichiometrically.
suggestions: Make the rxn_005 photoredox conditions explicit and tied to the reported Cu/H2S/UV chemistry.
Correct rxn_007 to mol_012 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_014 + mol_002 and consider splitting or annotating diastereomeric aminonitriles.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is very close to the experimentally supported core of the cyanosulfidic literature: rxn_005 and rxn_006 map directly onto the reported lactonitrile -> lactaldehyde -> aminonitrile chemistry. Confidence still drops at rxn_007 because free threonine hydrolysis was not reported and the written stoichiometry omits one H2O.
suggestions: Keep rxn_005 tied to the reported lactaldehyde-yield context rather than as a generic reduction.
Correct rxn_007 to include 2 H2O and specify the hydrolysis conditions needed to reach the amino acid.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: If lactaldehyde is available, Strecker capture is plausible; however the route still rests on rxn_007, the least supported step in the module. The network also pools threo/allo aminonitriles into mol_012, which weakens stereochemical bookkeeping.
suggestions: Define mol_012 as pooled threo/allo aminonitriles or split it into stereochemical nodes.
Add explicit hydrolysis conditions and correct rxn_007 stoichiometry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Chemically possible in principle, but this is the weakest standalone route in the network. Generic surface hydrolysis of the aminonitrile to free threonine is not established here, and rxn_007 needs a second water molecule to be correctly specified.
suggestions: Correct rxn_007 to mol_012 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_014 + mol_002.
Insert an amide or other hydrolysis intermediate and specify pH/temperature rather than leaving the step as a generic surface reaction.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The acetaldehyde-supply portion is plausible, and the Akabori step does make threonine experimentally, but only under Cu(II)-glycinate/basic preparative conditions that are not yet strongly prebiotic. Glycine is imported rather than generated within this pathway, so it works better as a module than as a closed synthesis.
suggestions: Provide in-network or explicitly external glycine provenance.
Annotate rxn_009/rxn_010 as a mixture-producing Cu/base equilibrium with an expected threo:allo ratio.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Shorter than P8, but still limited by the weakly prebiotic status of rxn_009 and by external glycine supply. Free threonine formation is experimentally real here, yet the environmental fit is only moderate because Cu, basicity, and concentration are not justified.
suggestions: Justify Cu(II), base, and concentration in a cool surface pool for rxn_009.
Link glycine supply to a supporting network or mark it clearly as an imported feed.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This has the best direct experimental support for producing free threonine, but also the weakest prebiotic contextualization. The reaction is reversible, should co-produce allothreonine, and needs explicit justification for Cu(II), base, and acetaldehyde concentration in the stated surface setting.
suggestions: State the expected threo:allo ratio and reversibility explicitly.
Justify Cu(II)-glycinate/basic conditions and acetaldehyde concentration geochemically.

evaluation.network_feedback: Connected, sufficiently populated network with consistent IDs and no atom/charge conservation failures in the supplied RDKit check. Literature alignment is a real strength: the network centers on the two reaction modules with actual threonine evidence, keeps allothreonine explicit, and includes retro-aldol loss. The main weaknesses are chemical and environmental: rxn_007 and rxn_008 are stoichiometrically incomplete as written and should be mol_012 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_014/mol_015 + mol_002; free-threonine release from the aminonitrile is not demonstrated in the cited cyanosulfidic work; rxn_002, rxn_003, and rxn_005 need explicit Cu-assisted UV/sulfide/phosphate conditions; and rxn_009/rxn_010 need clearer justification for Cu(II), basicity, concentration, and imported glycine. Also consider splitting mol_012 into threo/allo aminonitriles or labeling it as a pooled diastereomeric node, and tie rxn_011/rxn_012 rates to temperature/pH rather than a generic surface condition. Overall this is a coherent, literature-aware low-flux threonine network, but not yet a fully closed or experimentally validated end-to-end prebiotic synthesis.
